title: Serving runtime: architecture, kernel scheduling, profiling, benchmarking, and runbooks
author: Avery Chen
body:
Summary:

This document consolidates the serving runtime reference material for Redwood Inference: architecture overview, kernel scheduling design, profiling and benchmarking playbooks, release-note conventions, known issues, and operational runbooks. It is intended as the single-stop reference for on-call engineers, performance engineers, and anyone onboarding to the serving runtime team.

Scope:

- Runtime components maintained: router-service, inference-engine (gpu-exec), kv-cache, batching-service, model-manager, telemetry-proxy.
- Topics: design rationale, scheduling decisions, profiling tooling and standard runs, benchmark suite and golden metrics, release and rollout steps, common incidents and runbook steps, team wiki links and ownership.

1) Architecture overview

High-level goals:
- Provide predictable p99 latency SLOs for interactive routes (target p99 <= 300ms for small chat models on Dedicated pool).
- Optimize throughput for batch/embeddings workloads with cost-aware scheduling.
- Support model variants (quantized/int8, fp16) and automated fallback policies.

Core components and responsibilities:
- router-service: request routing, policy evaluation (latency/cost/region), auth, and initial request shaping.
- inference-engine (gpu-exec): GPU-optimized execution, KV cache management, attention kernel selection, and session lifecycle.
- batching-service: continuous batching and backpressure controllers.
- model-manager: artifact distribution, version pinning, warm-up, and health checks.
- kv-cache: shared prefix/KV cache service with LRU eviction and sharding by model-version.
- telemetry-proxy: aggregates token-level latency/cost traces and forwards to observability.

Design notes and trade-offs:
- Kernel selection is done per-sequence-length bucket at model load time with runtime fallbacks. This reduces per-request overhead but requires profiling the model across representative sequence distributions.
- Continuous batching favors latency SLOs by using a dynamic max-wait parameter tuned per route. See kernel-scheduling section for details.
- Caching is conservative for private deployments (on by default but configurable for regulatory customers).

2) Kernel scheduling and GPU execution model

Goals:
- Maximize GPU utilization while preserving latency SLOs for interactive traffic.
- Minimize kernel launch overhead and memory fragmentation.

Key mechanisms:
- Sequence-length bucketing: incoming requests are classified into buckets by effective sequence length (prompt + expected completion). Buckets map to preselected kernel/launch parameters.
- Kernel profile registry: model-manager stores a small set of kernel candidates for each model-version; each entry includes memory footprint, expected cycles/step, and warm-up cost.
- Work-stealing scheduler: each GPU worker maintains local queues per-bucket. If underutilized, it will steal compatible batches from neighboring workers to improve utilization.
- Continuous batching policy: dynamic batch size target = min(max_batch_by_bucket, floor(current_pending / active_workers)). A max-wait latency guard (default 20ms for interactive routes) ensures p99 safety.

Configuration knobs (default values):

| setting | default | notes |
|---|---:|---|
| max_batch_by_bucket | 64 | upper bound to avoid OOM with long sequences |
| max_wait_ms | 20 | legal interactive target; increased for high-throughput non-interactive routes |
| kv_cache_shard_count | 64 | per-model sharding to reduce lock contention |
| worker_steal_threshold | 5% | percent idle threshold for steal attempts |

Operational implications:
- Changing max_batch_by_bucket for a model requires a controlled rollout and a benchmark run (see Benchmarking Suite).
- Kernel profile updates (e.g., switching to a new fused-attention kernel) must be tested on representative traffic to avoid regression in p95/p99.

3) Profiling playbook (how we profile a model and diagnose perf regressions)

Overview:
This playbook defines the standard tooling and steps for profiling model performance end-to-end, from cold-start to steady-state. Use the profiling-job template in infra-ci and the perf-collector utility.

Preconditions:
- Test dataset (prompt set) validated by Applied ML with representative length distribution.
- Profiling infra: dedicated profiling pods with same hardware SKU as production.

Standard profiling steps:
1. Baseline capture: run three warm-up runs, then collect 10 steady-state runs for each sequence-length bucket.
2. Kernel-level trace: enable kernel tracing (gpu-exec --trace-kernels) to record launch times and kernel durations.
3. KV-cache experiment: run with cache enabled/disabled to quantify hit rate impact.
4. Memory pressure sweep: run increasing batch sizes to find peak memory and OOM threshold.
5. Network and routing overhead: run centralized router-service in the loop to measure end-to-end tail latency.

Artifacts to collect:
- per-token latency histograms (p50/p90/p95/p99), throughput (tokens/s), GPU utilization, kernel timeline (nvidia nsight or perf-collector output), and telemetry traces.

Common diagnostics and actions:
- High kernel-launch overhead: check if kernel selection is falling back to a generic implementation; consider pinning a specialized kernel in the registry or reducing kernel recompile churn.
- Low utilization with many small sequences: increase batch max_wait_ms for non-latency-critical routes or enable request coalescing in the router.
- Memory fragmentation/OOMs after model upgrade: ensure allocator tuning parameters and restart worker to reclaim GPU memory; consider upgrading to a newer allocator in release.

4) Benchmarking suite and golden metrics

Benchmark suite components:
- unit-bench: microbenchmarks for individual kernels and layers.
- seq-bench: end-to-end sequence latency and throughput across sequence-length buckets.
- scale-bench: distributed throughput test across N GPUs to validate scaling and work-stealing.
- cost-bench: simulated traffic mix to estimate $/1000 tokens under current batching/caching config.

Golden metrics (example targets; route-specific SLAs live in route config):
- interactive_small_chat (p99 latency): <= 300ms on Dedicated type-A (8xA100/80GB)
- embeddings_batch (throughput): > 2500 embeddings/s per 8xA100 cluster
- utilization (steady-state): GPU SM utilization >= 65% for throughput routes
- cost efficiency: <$0.003 per 1k tokens for common open-models using quantized profiles

Benchmarking process (numbered):
1. Create benchmark run using perf-ci template, pin model-version and kernel-profile.
2. Run seq-bench for each sequence-length bucket with cache enabled and disabled.
3. Collect artifacts and compare to golden baselines in the perf-dashboard.
4. If regression >10% p95 or >15% p99, open a performance-triage issue and follow triage guide.

5) Release notes and kernel/profile rollout procedure

Release conventions:
- All runtime releases use semantic versioning: runtime-x.y.z. Kernel-profile changes are separate artifacts (kernel-profile-<model>-vN).
- Every release must include: changelog, perf regression test summary, security notes, and rollout plan section.

Rollout steps for kernel/profile updates (safe default):
1. Internal canary: deploy to 5% of dedicated workers with perf-monitoring enabled for 24 hours.
2. Perf-check: automatically compare p50/p95/p99 to baseline; block on p99 regression >10%.
3. Gradual rollout: 5%, 25%, 50%, 100% with 1-hour observation windows between steps.
4. Automated rollback: if automated checks fail or on-call signals an incident, rollback to previous profile and notify SRE.

Ownership and approvals:
- Change owner: runtime-performance@redwood.internal (primary: Marcos Rivera).
- Approvers: runtime-leads and applied-ml (Priya Singh) must sign off for model-level kernel profile changes.

6) Known issues (current as of last_updated)

- Issue: sporadic p99 spikes when switching between long and short sequence workloads on same GPU pool. Workaround: create separate pools or enable aggressive preemption policy. Tracking ticket: PERF-4823.
- Issue: increased memory fragmentation after model hot-reload leading to OOMs in long-running workers. Mitigation: schedule rolling worker restarts during low-traffic windows. Tracking ticket: RUNTIME-3771.
- Issue: rare correctness regressions with newest fused-attention kernel on specific fp16 quantized models. Status: restricted rollout while applied-ml runs correctness suite. Tracking ticket: MODEL-2127.

7) Runbooks (common operational playbooks)

A. High p99 latency on interactive route
1. Confirm SLO breach: check telemetry p99 for route in last 5m vs baseline.
2. Identify scope: isolate by model-version, region, or pool.
3. Check GPU utilization: if low and many small requests, consider increasing max_wait_ms or scaling workers down/up.
4. If utilization is high and latency high, investigate kernel traces for long-running kernels and check for recent kernel-profile rollouts.
5. Mitigation steps (ordered): scale up dedicated pool, roll back kernel-profile, enable fast-fallback model variant.
6. Post-incident: open postmortem and attach profiling artifacts.

B. OOM on worker
1. Collect dmesg/gpu logs and worker logs.
2. Mark worker unhealthy in model-manager and evacuate sessions.
3. Restart worker and monitor memory patterns.
4. If reoccurs, reduce max_batch_by_bucket for affected model and schedule allocator tuning.

C. Regression detected in benchmarking CI
1. Stop rollout and notify runtime-performance@.
2. Run profiling playbook to reproduce locally.
3. If reproducible, revert to golden kernel-profile and create regression ticket for root cause.

- Applied ML owner for model validation: Priya Singh (priya.s@redwood.ai).
- Security contact for runtime CVEs: security@redwood.ai.

Appendices

A. Example commands
1. Run profiler locally:
```bash
# run perf collector against a model-version on local profiling cluster
perf-collector run --model gpt-open-7b --version v3 --buckets 32 --out /tmp/perf-run
```

2. Launch a canary rollout:
```bash
runtime-cli rollout kernel-profile --model gpt-open-7b --profile v3 --percent 5 --watch
```

B. Short checklist for model onboarding to runtime
- Validate artifact (sha256) and kernel-profile smoke tests.
- Run profiling playbook end-to-end and publish perf report.
- Add model to golden-bench registry and set initial route SLOs.
- Schedule canary rollout and obtain applied-ml sign-off.

C. References and tickets
- PERF-4823, RUNTIME-3771, MODEL-2127
